title: Universal Multiclass Transductive Online Learning
claim: A tree structure whose branches are consistent with concepts, with sibling edges required to carry distinct labels, captures the combinatorial core of learnability.
layout: 1 panel, left-to-right binary tree, one highlighted red branch with arrow
description: A single binary tree of depth 3 drawn left to right. The root x_0 is on the left. It branches into two x_1 nodes, and each of those branches into two x_2 nodes. Every x_2 node has two dashed edges that continue the tree. Edges carry integer labels: 1 and 2 at the root, 3 and 4, 5 and 6 at the next level, and 9 and 10, 9 and 10, 14 and 20, 3 and 4 on the dashed edges. The two edges leaving any node always have different labels. One branch is highlighted in thick red. It runs from x_0 through x_1 and x_2 to the final dashed edge labelled 20. A thin red curved arrow on the right points at that last edge. The eye goes first to the red path. The black tree is plain and uncluttered.

The only restriction is that the two edges connecting two children of the same node should be labeled with different labels. This is illustrated here for one of the branches.
abstract: We consider the problem of universal transductive online classification with a possibly unbounded label space. This setting considers online learning, with the sequence of instances (without labels) known to the learner in advance. We say a concept class $\mathcal{H}$ is learnable if there is a learning algorithm $\mathcal{A}$, such that for every realizable sequence, the number of mistakes made by $\mathcal{A}$ grows at most sublinearly with the number of predictions. We characterize the learnability of this setting and show that there are only two possible optimal rates for the learnable classes: either bounded or increasing logarithmically. We introduce a new combinatorial structure, called ``Level-Constrained-Littlestone-Littlestone (LCLL) tree'', which, along with the indifference property, characterizes the learnability. We also extend the learnability result to the agnostic case and the case where only the stochastic process that generates the instance sequence is known.
